title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a

references:

author: Clankerusecase

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
O-UNC-066 passkey-themed vishing phishing domain contact (assignpasskey/deploypasskey/etc.) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint/DNS resolution or connection to the five O-UNC-066 ('Pink') passkey-themed phishing domains used to lure Microsoft 365 users mid-vishing call into enrolling an attacker passkey. Article-specific because it pins the exact registered domain set rather than a generic phishing pattern. Rationale: Uses the five exact registered domains from the article's IOC block, all confirmed in Okta's primary write-up. Any resolution is a strong pre-compromise vishing signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness team detonating the phishing domains in a sandbox/test range
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the IOC domains during triage
  • URL-scanning/sandbox appliances auto-resolving reported domains
  • Corporate DNS sinkhole/RPZ probe traffic against known-bad lists
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and check whether it followed an inbound phone call or unusual sign-in; pull recent Entra sign-ins for that UPN. 2) Contain: force sign-out + revoke refresh tokens for the user, reset password, and quarantine any attacker-registered auth method (see UC2). 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy org-wide for all five domains and any *passkey* subdomains over 30d; cross-reference against Entra 'User registered security info' events in the same window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let PasskeyDomains = dynamic(["assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Name has_any (PasskeyDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue Entra passkey/FIDO2 registration from O-UNC-066 operator ASN (DDoS-Guard/IQWeb) AIInstallation High
Detects an attacker-driven passkey/security-key registration in Entra where the associated successful sign-in originated from the O-UNC-066 operator infrastructure ASNs (AS57724 DDoS-Guard, AS59692 IQWeb FZ-LLC). This is the core account-takeover persistence step — the operator logs in with harvested creds and enrolls their own passkey, surviving password/MFA resets. Rationale: Combines the article's account-takeover objective (attacker enrolls own passkey) with the corroborated operator ASNs from Okta's report; the temporal join of a suspect-ASN sign-in to a security-info registration removes the huge FP volume created by Microsoft's legitimate passkey adoption campaigns. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/coreinfrastructureandsecurityblog/auditing-fido2-authentication-for-windows-sign-in/4509702
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately enrolling a passkey during a Microsoft-driven registration campaign (from a corporate IP, not the suspect ASNs)
  • Help-desk admin registering security info on a user's behalf from an internal range
  • VPN egress that happens to share a hosting ASN (validate the specific IP, not just ASN)
  • Traveling employee on a hosting-provider mobile network
Suppression filter
| where OperatorIP !in (dynamic([])) // add validated corporate/VPN egress IPs sharing these ASNs to suppress
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the TargetUPN's full Entra sign-in + audit trail; confirm the registering IP maps to AS57724/AS59692 and identify the newly added authentication method (KeyIdentifier). 2) Contain: delete the rogue passkey/FIDO2 method, revoke all refresh tokens, reset password, and require re-registration of MFA from a trusted device; block the operator IP/ASN at conditional access. 3) Hunt: enumerate every passkey registered tenant-wide in the last 30d, flag any from non-corporate IPs; check the leak-site actor 'Pink' overlap and search for data-exfil/mailbox-rule creation on the affected account.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft Entra ID","Office 365","Azure Active Directory")
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","register security info","key credential")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("passkey","fido2","fido","Fido2")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectASN = dynamic([57724, 59692]); // AS57724 DDoS-Guard, AS59692 IQWeb FZ-LLC = O-UNC-066 hosting
let OperatorSignins = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AutonomousSystemNumber in (SuspectASN)
| project SignInTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, OperatorIP = IPAddress, ASN = AutonomousSystemNumber, AppDisplayName;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration","Add device-based key credential (user)")
| extend TargetUPN = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| where isnotempty(TargetUPN)
| join kind=inner OperatorSignins on $left.TargetUPN == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (SignInTime .. SignInTime + 1h)
| project RegistrationTime = TimeGenerated, TargetUPN, OperationName, SignInTime, OperatorIP, ASN, AppDisplayName
| order by RegistrationTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory (@evt.name:"User registered security info" OR @evt.name:"Admin registered security info" OR @evt.name:"Add device-based key credential (user)")
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.action="modified" AND All_Changes.command IN ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","Add device-based key credential (user)") by All_Changes.user All_Changes.src All_Changes.command _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | iplocation src | search Autonomous_System IN ("DDoS-Guard","IQWeb*") OR asn IN (57724,59692)
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.action="modified" AND All_Changes.command IN ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","Add device-based key credential (user)") by All_Changes.user All_Changes.src All_Changes.command _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | iplocation src | search Autonomous_System IN ("DDoS-Guard","IQWeb*") OR asn IN (57724,59692)
O-UNC-066 passkey phishing-kit URL-path fingerprint (/backend.php, /submit-authenticator, /passkey/check) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Safe-Links/proxy telemetry for the distinctive multi-stage URL paths of the operator-controlled PHP passkey phishing kit (real-time OTP relay + passkey-decoy pages). Catches per-target subdomains the domain-list UC (UC1) misses, because it keys on the kit's path structure rather than the registered domain. Rationale: The kit's fixed path sequence (/gate → /identify → /password → /backend.php → /processing → /submit-otp|/submit-authenticator|/approve-authenticator → /passkey/register → /passkey/check → /done) is enumerated in the article; requiring 'passkey' in the host plus a kit path keeps it specific to this campaign and catches fresh per-victim subdomains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment/
ATT&CKT1111 T1566.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate passkey-management SaaS whose paths coincidentally include /passkey/register or /passkey/check (validate the host)
  • Internal passkey pilot/enrollment portal hosted on a *passkey* subdomain
  • Red-team phishing simulation replaying the kit paths
  • Safe-Links rescanning a previously reported URL
Suppression filter
| where DestinationHostName !endswith "contoso.com" // exclude sanctioned internal passkey portal(s)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the clicking user and whether ActionType/IsClickedThrough shows they reached the page; check for an OTP-submission stage (/submit-otp, /submit-authenticator) indicating live credential/MFA relay. 2) Contain: revoke tokens + reset password for the user immediately (assume creds and OTP captured), and check for a subsequent passkey registration (UC2). 3) Hunt: extract the destination host and pivot org-wide for other users hitting the same host/path set; submit the host to takedown and add to the UC1 domain block list.
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where Url has "passkey"
| where Url has_any ("/backend.php","/submit-otp","/submit-authenticator","/approve-authenticator","/passkey/register","/passkey/check","/processing","/identify","/gate","/done")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, IPAddress, Workload, IsClickedThrough
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has "passkey"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/backend.php","/submit-otp","/submit-authenticator","/approve-authenticator","/passkey/register","/passkey/check","/processing","/identify","/gate","/done")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceUserName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Attackers Exploit 'Ill Bloom' Vulnerability to Drain Over $5 Million From Cryptocurrency Wallets

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 6 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Security firm&nbsp;Coinspect&nbsp;has disclosed a crypto wallet flaw it calls&nbsp;Ill Bloom, and attackers are already using it. The flaw is in how some wallet software generated its recovery phrase, the words that control the money. When that phrase is made with weak randomness, an attacker can work it out and take everything it controls. The firm has confirmed one coordinated sweep on May 27

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

            - '\brave.exe'

    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

description: |

    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.

    activity.

            - '\Electrum\wallets\'

            - '\Exodus.exe'

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'

level: high

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-56291")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

YesWiki CalcField eval() RCE: php/apache web process spawns shell or recon binary AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-52778 execution phase where a bypass of the CalcField.php regex sandbox reaches eval() and runs OS commands (PoC: abs(1) + system('id')). A PHP-FPM/Apache worker forking /bin/sh, id, whoami, uname, curl or wget is the tell that the math parser was weaponised into command execution as www-data. Rationale: Directly models the article's RCE PoC (abs(1) + system('id')) — a web interpreter (php-fpm/apache) is the parent and the child is a shell/recon binary; the parent constraint is what turns generic 'id ran' into a high-fidelity CVE-2026-52778 signal. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/yeswiki-rce-redos-in-bazar-calcfield-cve-2026-52778/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A YesWiki/PHP plugin legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick (convert) or ffmpeg for media processing
  • Backup or cron jobs run under the www-data account invoking bash wrapper scripts
  • CI/deploy tooling on the web host running composer post-install hooks that fork sh
  • Monitoring agents that php-exec 'uname'/'whoami' for host inventory
  • Webhook handlers that legitimately call curl/wget to fetch remote resources
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ImageMagick","convert ","ffmpeg") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "composer")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alerting host — confirm the php-fpm/apache parent's InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the child ProcessCommandLine; look for 'id','uname','curl' with no matching application feature. Correlate the timestamp with web access logs for a Bazar form-save request. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending php-fpm worker, and block the source IP at the WAF; take the YesWiki instance offline pending patch to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: on the same host search for new .php files in the webroot (webshell), www-data reads of /etc/passwd or .env, and outbound connections from php-fpm to attacker infrastructure.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

YesWiki post-RCE credential access: web user reads /etc/passwd or .env AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-52778 credential-access follow-on where code running as www-data reads local secret/identity files (/etc/passwd, .env, config.php, id_rsa) as called out in the advisory's impact section. Pivots on a PHP/Apache web process whose child command line references those secret paths. Rationale: Uses the advisory's explicit credential-access impact ("read sensitive system files e.g. /etc/passwd, .env") anchored to a web-server parent process, so it only fires when the web tier — not a legitimate admin shell — touches those secrets. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8

  • Admin troubleshooting a permissions issue by grepping /etc/passwd while su'd to www-data
  • Backup scripts run as www-data that archive the app directory including .env
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) runs touching /etc/passwd under the web user context
  • Security scanners fingerprinting the host that read /etc/passwd

| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","rsync","tar -") )

YesWiki webshell persistence: php/apache worker writes .php under Bazar webroot AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-52778 persistence step where the attacker uses eval() RCE to write a PHP backdoor into the YesWiki webroot (advisory: "modify application files, inject backdoors"). Fires when a PHP-FPM/Apache process creates or modifies a .php/.phtml file under the bazar/tools/yeswiki directories. Rationale: Anchored on the advisory's persistence impact ("inject backdoors") and the affected component path tools/bazar — a web worker (not a deploy pipeline) writing new .php files into its own served directory is a classic webshell drop. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • YesWiki's own Twig/template compile cache writing generated .php files under cache/ or tmp/
  • A legitimate in-app plugin/theme installer that unpacks .php files to the webroot
  • Admin-driven git pull / rsync deploy that runs as the web user and updates .php files
  • Composer autoload regeneration writing vendor .php files
  • WordPress/other CMS co-hosted on the same box writing plugin files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/cache/","/tmp/","/twig","/vendor/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file — a short file with eval/base64_decode/assert/system or $_POST/$_GET handlers confirms a webshell; compare its hash against known-good YesWiki files. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, isolate the host, block the source IP, and preserve a copy for forensics; patch to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: grep the whole webroot for other recently-modified .php files, check web access logs for GET/POST hits to the new path, and review UC1/UC2 for the initial command execution and secret theft.

YesWiki CVE-2026-52778 exploit request: Bazar formula with system() or nested-paren ReDoS AIDelivery Low
Hunts the initial-access/exploit HTTP request to a YesWiki Bazar CalcField carrying either the RCE marker system( or the deeply nested-parenthesis structure used for the PCRE stack-overflow DoS. Web-tier hunting query; grounded in the advisory's two PoC payloads. Rationale: Both PoC payloads from the advisory are used verbatim — the RCE string system( and the thousands-of-nested-parens ReDoS structure (matched as 6+ consecutive '('). Scoped to Bazar to cut noise; low confidence because the payload often lives in the POST body rather than the URL (false negatives), so pair with UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/yeswiki-rce-redos-in-bazar-calcfield-cve-2026-52778/ • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Bazar Calc field with a genuinely paren-heavy but valid math formula
  • Security scanners / DAST tooling probing the YesWiki instance with fuzz payloads
  • A WAF that URL-decodes and logs POST bodies producing benign 'system(' substrings in unrelated content
  • Copy-pasted formula documentation submitted through the form
  • Load-testing tools replaying recorded Bazar save requests
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (method, source IP, authenticated user, body if captured) and the HTTP status — a 5xx or dropped connection alongside a huge nested-paren body indicates a successful ReDoS crash; a 200 with system( suggests RCE attempt. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, add a rule rejecting Bazar formula fields exceeding a sane length / paren depth, and prioritise patching to YesWiki >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: on the target host correlate with UC1 (php spawning shell), php-fpm worker segfaults/restarts in syslog, and new webshell files (UC3) from the same source IP or session.

| where Url has "bazar"
| where Url contains "system(" or Url matches regex @"\({6,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki CVE-2026-52777 BazarImport POST to ?BazaR&vue=importer (CSRF exploit request) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to the YesWiki BazaR importer endpoint (`?BazaR&vue=importer&id_typeannonce=<N>`) carrying the `importfiche` parameter — the exact request shape that reaches the CSRF-able `CSVManager::importEntry` unserialize sink. Article-specific because it keys on the literal action route and POST parameter, not a generic web-import template; a cross-site Referer or missing CSRF token on this route is the CVE-2026-52777 tell. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit route `?BazaR&vue=importer&id_typeannonce=` and the `importfiche` POST parameter from BazarImportAction::formatArguments(); the CSRF path means the request will often carry an external Referer, which raises fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate wiki admin performing a genuine Bazar CSV import via the UI
  • Automated content-migration scripts that batch-import Bazar entries
  • Security scanners / vuln management probing the importer endpoint
  • Same-origin admin activity where Referer is the wiki itself (filter with CrossSiteRef)
Suppression filter
| where CrossSiteRef == "cross-site" or isempty(Referer)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request — decode the `importfiche[0]` value; if it base64-decodes to a PHP-serialized blob (`a:`/`O:` prefix) it is an exploit attempt, benign UI imports send CSV rows not serialized objects. Check Referer/source IP against known admin workstations. 2) Contain: if the request succeeded (2xx) treat the host as potentially RCE-compromised — isolate the web server, invalidate all admin sessions, and rotate the admin credential. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to php-fpm/apache child-process spawns and new `.php` file writes in the web root within minutes of this request; confirm YesWiki is >= 4.6.6.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "BazaR" and Url has "vue=importer"
| extend Referer = column_ifexists("HttpRequestHeaderReferer", "")
| extend CrossSiteRef = iff(Referer matches regex @"(?i)^https?://" and not(Referer has DstHostname), "cross-site", "same-site-or-none")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent = column_ifexists("HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent",""), Referer, CrossSiteRef
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki BazarImport base64 PHP-serialized object payload in POST body (PHPGGC gadget) AIExploitation High
Higher-fidelity variant that inspects the request body for the `importfiche` parameter carrying a base64 blob that decodes to a PHP-serialized object — i.e. a PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 or FW1 gadget chain. Keys on the serialized-object base64 signatures (`Tzo` = `O:`, `YTox`/`YToy` = `a:1:`/`a:2:`) seen in the advisory PoC payload, so it fires on the actual deserialization exploit rather than benign CSV imports. Rationale: Combines the article's `importfiche` parameter with the base64 signatures of PHP-serialized objects (`Tzo`=`O:`, `YToxOnt`=`a:1:{`) matching the verbatim PoC payload `YToxOntpOjA7Tzo2...`; benign CSV imports never carry serialized objects, giving low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190 T1027
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A pentester/red-team validating CVE-2026-52777 with a real PHPGGC payload (true positive that is authorised)
  • Security researcher sending the advisory's exact PoC base64 marker for testing
  • WAF logging a blocked deserialization attempt (still worth alerting — attack occurred)
  • Rare CSV cell content that coincidentally base64-matches the serialized signature (mitigated by requiring the importfiche param)
Response runbook
1) Triage: base64-decode the captured `importfiche` value; confirm it deserializes to a PHP object graph (look for `O:<len>:"<class>"` and Doctrine gadget class names). 2) Contain: assume RCE if the server responded 2xx — isolate the web host, kill/rotate the web-app service account, invalidate admin sessions, and snapshot for forensics before rebuild. 3) Hunt: correlate with php-fpm/apache spawning a shell and web-shell `.php` writes within 2s of this request; sweep other admin accounts and shared-hosting neighbours mentioned as pivot targets in the advisory.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki object-injection RCE: php-fpm/apache spawns shell (Doctrine/RCE1 system()) AIExploitation High
Detects a PHP web-server process (php-fpm, php, php-cgi, httpd, apache2, or w3wp hosting PHP) spawning a command shell — the terminal behaviour of the PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 gadget that ends in `system($cmd)` after CVE-2026-52777 deserialization. Article-specific because the advisory names the RCE1 gadget and the sink executes in the web-server process context. Rationale: The advisory states the Doctrine/RCE1 gadget terminates in `system($cmd)`; a web-server PHP process spawning sh/bash/cmd is the highest-fidelity post-exploitation signal and named binaries make this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • YesWiki/PHP app legitimately shelling out (e.g. ImageMagick, git, or backup cron invoked via exec)
  • Composer/plugin install running shell commands as the web user
  • Server monitoring plugins that call system utilities
  • Admin debugging via a PHP web shell they deployed intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs","gm","/usr/bin/git","composer"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child process command line — benign PHP shell-outs are narrow known utilities; arbitrary `sh -c`, recon (`id`,`whoami`,`uname`), or download commands (`curl`,`wget`) indicate exploitation. Correlate timestamp with a preceding `vue=importer` POST. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, terminate the shell tree, suspend the web-app service account, and preserve memory/disk. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web user (web shells, cron entries), check outbound connections from the PHP process, and confirm all YesWiki instances are patched to 4.6.6.

YesWiki BazarImport RCE: PHP process writes web shell or tampers wakka.config.php AIInstallation Medium
Detects the YesWiki web-server process writing a `.php` file into the web root or modifying `wakka.config.php` — the outcome of the PHPGGC Doctrine/FW1 gadget (`file_put_contents($php_file, $contents)`) and the persistence actions the advisory explicitly calls out (web shells, wakka.config.php modification). Article-specific through the named config file and the FW1 file-write primitive. Rationale: Uses the advisory's named `wakka.config.php` config file and the Doctrine/FW1 `file_put_contents($php_file)` primitive; a web-server PHP process writing a new .php outside cache/tmp is a strong web-shell indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • YesWiki extension/theme installation writing new .php files under the web root
  • Legitimate admin editing wakka.config.php via the wiki configuration UI
  • YesWiki cache/compiled-template regeneration (mitigated by excluding cache/tmp paths)
  • Composer autoloader regeneration during an upgrade
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "/tools/" and FolderPath !has "/vendor/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file — a small file with `eval`, `system`, `assert`, `base64_decode`, or `$_POST`/`$_GET` handlers is a web shell; diff wakka.config.php against the last known-good backup for injected handlers or altered secrets. 2) Contain: remove/quarantine the file, block web access to it, rotate any secrets exposed in wakka.config.php (DB creds), and invalidate admin sessions. 3) Hunt: search web access logs for GETs to the new .php filename (attacker interaction), review all files owned by the web user modified in the exploit window, and confirm the YesWiki upgrade to 4.6.6.

YesWiki deserialization exploit failures in PHP/web error logs (unserialize / __destruct) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts PHP or web-server error logs for the deserialization exploit's failure fingerprints — `unserialize` warnings, magic-method errors, and specifically the PoC's `Object of class ... could not be converted to string` message thrown by the `array_map('strval', $entry)` line at CSVManager.php:373. Failed or version-mismatched PHPGGC chains against CVE-2026-52777 surface here, often repeating as the attacker retries. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim PoC error `Object of class Gadget could not be converted to string` produced by the CSVManager `array_map('strval', $entry)` line, plus `unserialize`/`__destruct` magic-method fingerprints — exactly what a failed or mistuned gadget chain emits. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated PHP plugin bugs that legitimately call unserialize and warn on malformed data
  • Developers running/debugging code that emits __destruct or serialization notices
  • Batch import of a genuinely malformed (but non-malicious) CSV/serialized cache file
  • Noisy verbose logging levels producing routine deprecation notices
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("could not be converted to string", "unserialize")
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the error timestamp with web access logs for a `vue=importer` POST from the same source IP; a burst of these errors near an importer request indicates active exploitation attempts. 2) Contain: if paired with a successful (2xx) import request, treat as compromise — isolate host and rotate the web-app service account. 3) Hunt: enumerate retry attempts (repeated errors) to gauge attacker persistence, then pivot to php->shell spawns and new .php writes on the same host; verify YesWiki is patched to 4.6.6 which removes the serialized-transport path.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("unserialize", "could not be converted to string", "__destruct", "__wakeup", "Object of class")
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:(php OR php-fpm OR apache2 OR httpd) ("unserialize" OR "could not be converted to string" OR "__destruct" OR "__wakeup" OR "Object of class")

YesWiki bulk page deletion via {{erasespamedcomments}} — audit-log deletion burst AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a burst of YesWiki 'Suppression de la page' administrative-action log entries in a short window, the ground-truth impact signal of CVE-2026-52766 where a single POST with a multi-element suppr[] array deletes many wiki pages at once. Keys on the exact French audit string LogAdministrativeAction writes for each deleted tag. Rationale: Uses the exact 'Suppression de la page' string that PageController::delete() -> LogAdministrativeAction writes for every deleted tag; a burst of >=3 in 5 minutes reflects the suppr[] array bulk-delete described in the article and CVSS A:H impact. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52766/
ATT&CKT1485
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin decommissioning a section of the wiki and deleting several pages in one sitting
  • Site migration or content restructuring where old pages are pruned in bulk
  • Genuine spam cleanup by an authorized moderator using the same action against real spam pages
  • Automated maintenance/cron job that prunes stale draft pages
Suppression filter
| where DeletedPages >= 3
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SamplePages set and confirm whether high-value tags (PagePrincipale, admin/config pages) were deleted; check the web/WAF log for the source IP of the POST to the trigger page immediately preceding the burst. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the wiki read-only, and restore deleted rows from the latest DB backup (pages/links/acls/triples/referrers/tags). 3) Hunt: confirm YesWiki version <4.6.6, search for anonymously-created trigger pages containing '{{erasespamedcomments}}', and review for other unauth actions from the same IP.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where SyslogMessage has "Suppression de la page"     // exact LogAdministrativeAction string per deleted tag
| summarize DeletedPages = dcount(SyslogMessage), SamplePages = make_set(SyslogMessage, 15), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DeletedPages >= 3     // 3+ page deletions in 5 min = suppr[] array abuse, not routine one-off admin cleanup
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog "Suppression de la page"

| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*erasespamedcomments*" OR (Web.url="*clean=yes*" AND Web.url="*suppr*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count>=1
YesWiki CVE-2026-52766 exploit request — erasespamedcomments clean=yes suppr[] POST AIExploitation Medium
Detects the exploitation POST for CVE-2026-52766 in WAF/web request logs: a POST carrying the erasespamedcomments action together with the clean=yes flag and a suppr[] array. Requires request-body inspection on the WAF (the parameters live in the POST body, not the URL query string). Rationale: Keys on the three attacker-controlled strings from the article PoC (erasespamedcomments action name, clean=yes flag, suppr[] array); the combination is not produced by normal wiki browsing/editing. Confidence is Medium because the params sit in the POST body, so it only fires where the WAF logs request bodies. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52766/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An authorized moderator legitimately running the erasespamedcomments spam-cleanup action against genuine spam pages
  • WAF/vulnerability scanners (Nuclei, Burp) probing for CVE-2026-52766 in an authorized pentest
  • Security team validating the 4.6.6 patch with a benign reproduction request
  • Log-replay or SIEM test harness re-ingesting the PoC payload
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the suppr[] tags in the body to see which pages were targeted (PagePrincipale = front page) and check the response code/size to gauge success; verify the source IP is not an authorized admin. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and add a WAF rule denying POSTs containing clean=yes+suppr[] to unauthenticated sessions; upgrade YesWiki to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: correlate with Syslog 'Suppression de la page' entries within 60s to confirm pages were actually deleted, and review the same IP for other YesWiki CVEs from this advisory batch (SQLi, SSRF, eval RCE).
